title: Uzaktan çalışmanın ikinci perdesi
titleEn: The Second Act of Remote Work
text: When offices closed in 2020, remote work was presented as a straightforward victory: no commute, fewer interruptions, more autonomy. Five years later the picture is considerably more complicated. Productivity data from large firms suggests that individual output often rose, particularly for tasks that can be completed alone. What fell was something harder to measure. Junior employees, who once learned by overhearing experienced colleagues solve problems, reported that they had no idea how decisions were actually made. Informal knowledge, the kind that never appears in a manual, stopped circulating. Several companies responded by requiring three days in the office, a compromise that satisfied almost nobody. Employees who had moved to cheaper cities felt betrayed; managers argued that a team which never meets eventually stops behaving like a team. The more thoughtful organizations have stopped asking how many days people should attend and started asking what an office is actually for. If it exists to provide a desk, it has already lost to the kitchen table. If it exists to make collaboration and learning visible, then the question becomes which specific activities deserve the journey. That reframing is uncomfortable, because it requires managers to justify their own routines rather than simply reinstate them.

questions.note: "Individual output often rose, particularly for tasks that can be completed alone."

questions.q: What did junior employees lose?
options: Informal knowledge about how decisions are made
questions.note: "They had no idea how decisions were actually made."

questions.q: How did employees react to the three-day rule?
options: Those who had moved away felt betrayed
questions.note: "Employees who had moved to cheaper cities felt betrayed."

questions.q: What better question does the text propose?
options: What an office is actually for
questions.note: "Started asking what an office is actually for."

questions.q: Why is that question uncomfortable for managers?
options: They must justify their own routines
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Restoran eleştirisinin sonu
titleEn: The End of the Restaurant Critic
text: For most of the twentieth century a single newspaper critic could determine whether a restaurant survived its first year. The critic visited anonymously, paid for the meal and published a judgment that carried the authority of the newspaper behind it. That arrangement has quietly collapsed. Today a restaurant is judged by thousands of customers who photograph every dish before eating it, and the average of their opinions appears on a map before anyone has finished dessert. The change is genuinely democratic, but it has consequences that are rarely discussed. Because a single angry review can lower a score noticeably, owners have strong incentives to avoid anything that might divide opinion. Unusual dishes, uncomfortable chairs and challenging flavors are quietly removed. What survives is what nobody objects to. Some chefs have adapted by designing food that photographs well, which is not the same as food that tastes good. A number of critics argue that their profession still matters precisely because it is not an average: one informed voice, willing to be wrong in public, can defend a difficult restaurant that a crowd would punish. Whether readers still want that voice is a separate question, and the evidence is not encouraging.

questions.q: What could a newspaper critic once determine?
options: Whether a restaurant survived its first year
questions.note: İlk cümle.

questions.q: What is the consequence of many small reviews?
questions.note: "Owners have strong incentives to avoid anything that might divide opinion."

questions.q: What does the text say survives?
questions.note: "What survives is what nobody objects to."

questions.q: How have some chefs adapted?
options: By designing food that photographs well
questions.note: "Designing food that photographs well."

questions.q: Why do critics argue their work still matters?
options: One informed voice is not an average
questions.note: "Precisely because it is not an average."

title: Deprem sonrası bir kasaba
text: Three years after the earthquake, the town of Demirkoy has been rebuilt, and the result satisfies almost nobody. The new houses are safer than anything that stood before; engineers inspected every foundation and the standards applied were unusually strict. Yet the population has fallen by a third. Families who lost their homes were housed temporarily in a city ninety kilometers away, and by the time the new buildings were ready, many of their children had started school there and their parents had found work. Returning would have meant a second disruption, this time voluntary. Those who did come back complain less about the buildings than about the arrangement of the streets. The old town had narrow lanes where neighbors met by accident; the new plan has wide roads designed for emergency vehicles, and people now drive past one another. The municipality points out, reasonably, that those wide roads exist because ambulances could not reach the old center. Nobody disputes the logic. The difficulty is that safety was measurable and community was not, so one of them shaped the plan and the other did not.

questions.q: What is true about the new houses?
options: They are safer than the old ones
questions.note: "The new houses are safer than anything that stood before."

questions.q: Why did many families not return?
options: The new houses were too expensive
Their children had started school elsewhere
questions.note: Çocuklar orada okula başlamış, ebeveynler iş bulmuştu.

questions.q: What do returning residents complain about most?
questions.note: "They complain less about the buildings than about the arrangement of the streets."

questions.q: Why are the new roads wide?
questions.note: "Ambulances could not reach the old center."

questions.q: What is the central difficulty in the final sentence?
options: Safety could be measured and community could not
questions.note: Ölçülebilen plana yön verdi, ölçülemeyen vermedi.

title: Ücretsiz staj tartışması
text: Defenders of unpaid internships usually make a reasonable-sounding argument: the student gains experience, the company takes a risk on somebody untested, and no money changes hands in either direction. The difficulty becomes obvious as soon as you ask who can accept such an offer. A student whose family can cover three months of rent in an expensive city can afford to work for nothing. A student who supports a younger sibling cannot, regardless of ability. Over time, entire professions become filled with people who were able to work without payment at twenty-two, which is a poor method of selecting talent and an efficient method of reproducing privilege. Some countries have responded with regulation, requiring that any internship lasting more than a few weeks must be paid at least the minimum wage. Employers warned that the number of opportunities would collapse. In practice the number fell modestly and the quality improved, because a company that must pay an intern has an incentive to give that intern real work rather than photocopying. The remaining problem is enforcement: in sectors where competition for entry is fierce, students rarely complain, and a rule that nobody reports is close to no rule at all.

questions.q: What is the argument of defenders?
options: Experience is exchanged for a risk, with no money either way
questions.note: İlk cümle.

questions.q: Which student cannot accept an unpaid offer?
options: One who supports a younger sibling
questions.note: "A student who supports a younger sibling cannot, regardless of ability."

questions.q: What does the practice reproduce, according to the text?
questions.note: "An efficient method of reproducing privilege."

questions.q: What actually happened after regulation?
options: Numbers fell modestly and quality improved
questions.note: "The number fell modestly and the quality improved."

questions.q: What is the remaining problem?
questions.note: "A rule that nobody reports is close to no rule at all."

title: Kaybolan el yazısı
text: Several education systems have quietly reduced the time devoted to handwriting, on the grounds that children will spend their working lives typing. The reasoning is practical and, on the surface, difficult to argue with. Research on how writing affects memory, however, complicates the picture. In a series of studies, students who took notes by hand performed better on questions requiring understanding than students who typed, even though the typists recorded considerably more words. The explanation offered is that handwriting is slow. Because you cannot possibly record everything, you are forced to decide what matters, and that decision is itself a form of learning. Typing, being fast enough to capture a lecture almost verbatim, allows the listener to postpone thinking indefinitely. None of this proves that handwriting should be protected at all costs; the studies involved small groups, and a skilled typist who summarizes rather than transcribes may well do better than either. But it does suggest that the choice is not merely about speed, and that a curriculum which treats writing purely as a technology for storing words may be removing something it never intended to touch.

questions.q: Why have some systems reduced handwriting lessons?
options: Children will spend their working lives typing
questions.note: İlk cümle.

questions.q: What did the studies find?
questions.note: "Students who took notes by hand performed better on questions requiring understanding."

questions.q: What explanation is offered?
options: Slowness forces you to decide what matters
questions.note: "Because you cannot possibly record everything, you are forced to decide what matters."

questions.q: What limitation does the text admit?
questions.note: "The studies involved small groups."

questions.q: What is the author's final point?
options: Handwriting must be protected at all costs
The choice is not merely about speed
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Müzede kimin hikâyesi
titleEn: Whose Story Does the Museum Tell?
text: A museum label appears to be a neutral piece of information: a name, a date, a material. In practice every label is the end of a long argument. When a regional museum recently reopened, the curators discovered that the collection had been described in the 1950s in language that no longer seemed defensible. Objects taken during a military campaign were listed as having been acquired, and the people who made them appeared only as anonymous craftsmen. Rewriting the labels sounds straightforward until you attempt it. Saying too little leaves the old impression intact; saying too much turns a display case into an essay that few visitors will read. The museum eventually settled on a compromise. Each label states plainly how the object entered the collection, in one sentence, and a longer explanation is available to anyone who wants it. Attendance has not fallen, and the letters of complaint were outnumbered by letters of thanks. The curators are careful, however, not to claim that the problem is solved. They point out that the new labels were written by the same institution that wrote the old ones, and that no amount of careful wording changes who currently holds the objects.

questions.q: What did the curators discover?
options: The old descriptions were no longer defensible
questions.note: 1950'lerdeki dil artık savunulabilir görünmüyordu.

questions.q: How were the original makers described?
questions.note: "The people who made them appeared only as anonymous craftsmen."

questions.q: What is the problem with saying too much on a label?
questions.note: "Turns a display case into an essay that few visitors will read."

questions.q: What compromise did the museum reach?
options: One plain sentence, with more available on request
questions.note: Tek cümlelik açık ifade, isteyene daha uzun açıklama.

questions.q: Why do the curators refuse to say the problem is solved?
options: The same institution still holds the objects
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Algoritmanın önerdiği şarkı
text: Music services promise to understand your taste better than you do, and to a remarkable degree they succeed. The system observes which songs you finish, which you skip after nine seconds, and what you play on a Tuesday morning as opposed to a Friday night. From these signals it builds a model that reliably produces music you enjoy. The criticism is not that the recommendations are bad, but that they are too well aimed. A listener who is never offered anything uncomfortable will never discover that their taste could have been different. Record shops and radio presenters were inefficient by comparison: they wasted your time with music you did not want, and occasionally that waste changed your life. Some services have tried to build surprise back in, adding a proportion of unfamiliar tracks to each playlist. The results have been mixed, largely because engineered surprise is measured by whether the listener stays, which quietly turns the unfamiliar track into another tool for keeping attention. Genuine discovery may require an institution that does not benefit from your continued listening, and it is not obvious who would pay for that.

questions.q: What does the system observe?
options: Which songs you finish or skip
questions.note: "Which songs you finish, which you skip after nine seconds."

questions.q: What is the criticism in the text?
options: The recommendations are too well aimed
questions.note: "Not that the recommendations are bad, but that they are too well aimed."

questions.q: Why were record shops described as inefficient?
options: They wasted your time with unwanted music
questions.note: "They wasted your time with music you did not want."

questions.q: What problem does engineered surprise have?
options: It is measured by whether the listener stays
questions.note: Sürpriz de dikkat tutma aracına dönüşüyor.

questions.q: What might genuine discovery require?
options: An institution that does not profit from your listening
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Gece treni geri döndü
titleEn: The Return of the Night Train
text: For two decades the night train looked like a museum piece. Budget airlines were faster and cheaper, and one European operator after another withdrew its sleeper services. The reversal, when it came, was driven less by nostalgia than by arithmetic. As the cost of short flights began to include their environmental damage, and as city centers introduced restrictions on early-morning flights, the comparison changed. A traveler who leaves at ten in the evening and arrives at seven in the morning has also avoided a hotel bill, which alters the calculation considerably. New services now run across several borders, and most of them are full. The obstacles are no longer commercial but technical. Each country operates its own signalling system, and a train crossing three of them needs equipment and staff certified for all three. Rolling stock is scarce, since the old carriages were sold or scrapped and new ones take years to build. Operators are therefore expanding slowly, which frustrates passengers but probably protects the revival: a service that runs late every night would lose the goodwill it has taken twenty years to rebuild.

questions.q: Why did operators withdraw sleeper services?
options: Budget airlines were faster and cheaper
questions.note: İkinci cümle.

questions.q: What drove the reversal?
questions.note: "Driven less by nostalgia than by arithmetic."

questions.q: What extra saving does a night train offer?
questions.note: "Has also avoided a hotel bill."

questions.q: What is the main obstacle now?
questions.note: "The obstacles are no longer commercial but technical."

questions.q: Why may slow expansion be a good thing?
options: Late trains would destroy the rebuilt goodwill
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Sınavın ölçtüğü şey
text: Every national examination carries an unspoken promise: that it measures ability rather than circumstance. The promise is never entirely kept. Research across several countries has repeatedly shown that results correlate with family income, and the usual explanation, private tuition, accounts for only part of the gap. A quieter factor is familiarity with the format. A student who has practiced sixty past papers is not necessarily better at the subject, but is much better at the examination, and those two things are easy to confuse. Some systems have responded by making past papers freely available, which helps but does not equalise, since the scarce resource is not the paper but the adult who explains what went wrong. Others have reduced the weight of the final exam and included work completed during the year, a change that introduces its own problem: coursework can be assisted at home, and the assistance is distributed as unevenly as everything else. There is no arrangement that removes advantage entirely. The honest position is to state clearly which advantages a particular system tolerates, rather than to claim that it has none.

questions.q: What is the unspoken promise of an exam?
options: It is the same for everyone
It measures ability rather than circumstance
questions.note: İlk cümle.

questions.q: What does private tuition explain?
options: The gap in one country only
questions.note: "Accounts for only part of the gap."

questions.q: What is the quieter factor?
questions.note: "A quieter factor is familiarity with the format."

questions.q: Why does publishing past papers not equalise results?
options: The scarce resource is the adult who explains mistakes
questions.note: Kıt olan kâğıt değil, hatayı açıklayan yetişkin.

questions.q: What does the author call the honest position?
options: Stating which advantages the system tolerates
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Bir dilin son konuşanı
titleEn: The Last Speaker of a Language
text: Linguists estimate that a language stops being spoken somewhere in the world every two weeks. The phrase "last speaker" is misleading, because a language rarely ends with a single person; it ends earlier, on the day the last two speakers who could hold a conversation are separated. After that the survivor has the vocabulary but nowhere to use it, and vocabulary without conversation decays quickly. Documentation projects record what they can, and the recordings are valuable, but a dictionary preserves a language in roughly the way a photograph preserves a person. What disappears is not only words. Many small languages encode information that the surrounding major language does not: precise terms for local plants, for the behavior of the sea in particular months, for relationships between families. Communities that decide to revive a language face a difficult choice, because reviving it means standardizing it, and standardization always favors one village's version over another's. Several revivals have nevertheless succeeded, usually where the language acquired a practical role — a school, a radio station, a workplace — rather than being preserved out of duty alone.

questions.q: Why is 'last speaker' misleading?
options: A language ends when the last two speakers are separated
questions.note: İkinci cümle.

questions.q: What happens to the survivor's vocabulary?
questions.note: "Vocabulary without conversation decays quickly."

questions.q: What comparison is made about dictionaries?
questions.note: "In roughly the way a photograph preserves a person."

questions.q: What kind of knowledge can small languages carry?
options: Precise local terms the major language lacks
questions.note: Yerel bitkiler, denizin davranışı, akrabalık ilişkileri.

questions.q: When have revivals usually succeeded?
options: When the language gained a practical role
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Sıfır atık mağazası
text: A shop that sells food without packaging looks like an obvious improvement, and in one respect it is: the containers that would have been thrown away simply never exist. What the early enthusiasm missed is that packaging does more than one job. It carries the date, it keeps air out, and it makes the product identical wherever it is bought. Remove it and each of those jobs has to be done another way or accepted as a loss. Shops of this kind report that their waste of the food itself is higher than in an ordinary supermarket, because rice left in an open container for three weeks does not keep as well as rice in a sealed bag. The honest accounting is therefore less flattering than the photographs suggest, though it is still probably favorable overall. What has proved harder to solve is convenience. A customer must remember to bring containers, and the shops that survive are the ones that accept this and sell jars at the door rather than lecturing the person who forgot. Several owners now say the environmental argument was never their strongest one. The shops that last are the ones where the food is simply better, and the absence of packaging is a reason to stay rather than a reason to come.

questions.q: What does the writer say packaging also does?
options: Carries the date and keeps air out
questions.note: "It carries the date, it keeps air out."

questions.q: Why is food waste higher in such shops?
options: Open containers do not keep food as well
questions.note: "Rice left in an open container for three weeks does not keep as well."

questions.q: What is the writer's view of the overall accounting?
options: Less flattering but still probably favorable
questions.note: "Less flattering than the photographs suggest, though it is still probably favorable."

questions.q: What do the surviving shops do about forgotten containers?
questions.note: "Sell jars at the door rather than lecturing the person who forgot."

questions.q: What do several owners now say?
options: Customers do not care about waste
The environmental argument was never their strongest
questions.note: "The environmental argument was never their strongest one."

title: Yorumların güvenilirliği
text: Most people now consult reviews before buying almost anything, and most people also know that a proportion of those reviews are not genuine. What is less widely understood is that the fake ones are rarely the problem. A paid review is usually clumsy, and readers have become good at spotting the enthusiasm that arrives three days after the product launches. The subtler difficulty lies in who chooses to write at all. Satisfied customers are largely silent; the people who take the time are those who were delighted or furious. A product with a genuine five-star average may simply have annoyed nobody enough to provoke a paragraph. Worse, the average conceals the shape of the distribution: a restaurant where half the visits are excellent and half are unacceptable scores the same as one that is reliably ordinary, and the second is by far the safer choice for a birthday. Experienced readers have adapted. They ignore the number, read the three-star reviews, which tend to be the most careful, and look for complaints that repeat. A single furious review tells you about one evening. The same complaint in four separate months tells you about the kitchen.

questions.q: Why are fake reviews rarely the main problem?
options: They are usually easy to spot
There are very few of them
questions.note: "A paid review is usually clumsy."

questions.q: What is the subtler difficulty?
options: Who chooses to write at all
questions.note: "The subtler difficulty lies in who chooses to write at all."

questions.q: What does an average conceal?
questions.note: "The average conceals the shape of the distribution."

questions.q: Which restaurant does the writer call safer?
questions.note: "The second is by far the safer choice for a birthday."

questions.q: What do experienced readers do?
options: Read three-star reviews and look for repeated complaints
questions.note: "Read the three-star reviews... and look for complaints that repeat."

title: Emeklilikten sonraki ilk yıl
text: Retirement is planned almost entirely in financial terms, which is understandable, since money is the part that can be calculated. The part that cannot be calculated causes more trouble. Studies that follow people through the first year after leaving work find a consistent pattern: three or four months of genuine pleasure, followed by a decline that surprises almost everyone who experiences it. The explanation is not that people miss the work. Very few do. What they miss is structure, and a supply of low-effort social contact that they never had to arrange. A working day delivers perhaps twenty small exchanges without any planning at all, and replacing them requires an effort that feels undignified to organize. Those who do best tend to have one fixed commitment involving other people that they cannot quietly drop: a class that meets at a set hour, a team that expects them, a grandchild collected on Thursdays. The commitment matters more than the activity. Financial advisers have begun, cautiously, to raise this with clients, though several report that the question lands badly. A person who has spent a decade calculating a pension does not always welcome being asked who they will speak to on a Tuesday.

questions.q: Why is retirement planned financially?
options: Money is the only thing that matters
Money is the part that can be calculated
questions.note: "Money is the part that can be calculated."

questions.q: What pattern do studies find?
options: Pleasure for months, then a decline
questions.note: "Three or four months of genuine pleasure, followed by a decline."

questions.q: What do people actually miss?
questions.note: "What they miss is structure, and a supply of low-effort social contact."

questions.q: What helps most, according to the text?
options: A fixed commitment involving other people
questions.note: "One fixed commitment involving other people that they cannot quietly drop."

questions.q: How do clients react to the question?
questions.note: "Several report that the question lands badly."

title: Çok dilli çocuk
text: Parents raising a child in two languages are given a great deal of contradictory advice, much of it delivered with more confidence than the evidence supports. The most persistent worry is that the child will be delayed. Children in this situation do often produce their first sentences slightly later and mix the two systems for a period, which alarms relatives. Both effects disappear, and by school age the child's total vocabulary across both languages is normal or better. The genuine risk is different and rarely mentioned. A second language survives only where it is needed, and a child works out very quickly which language is optional. If the parent understands the majority language, the child will answer in it, and within two years the second language becomes something the child comprehends but does not speak. Families who avoid this are not the ones with the best method; they are the ones with a genuine reason. A grandmother who speaks no English is worth more than any amount of determination, because she makes the language necessary rather than virtuous. Those without such a reason often manufacture one, and the ones who succeed tend to admit that the manufacturing never stops.

questions.q: What is the most persistent worry?
options: That the child will be confused for life
That the child will be delayed
questions.note: "The most persistent worry is that the child will be delayed."

questions.q: What does the writer say about that worry?
options: The effects disappear by school age
It applies only to some families
questions.note: "Both effects disappear, and by school age the child's total vocabulary... is normal or better."

questions.q: What is the genuine risk?
options: The child mixes the systems for ever
The child stops speaking the optional language
questions.note: "A child works out very quickly which language is optional."

questions.q: What makes a second language survive?
options: A genuine reason to need it
questions.note: "A second language survives only where it is needed."

questions.q: Why is the grandmother valuable?
questions.note: "She makes the language necessary rather than virtuous."

title: Açık ofis deneyi
text: The open office was sold on a simple promise. Remove the walls and colleagues will talk to one another, ideas will travel, and the accidental meeting will replace the scheduled one. The promise was tested properly for the first time only recently, when researchers fitted staff with badges that recorded who spoke to whom, before and after a company removed its internal walls. Face-to-face conversation fell by roughly seventy per cent. Electronic messages rose sharply. The employees had not become less social; they had become less willing to be overheard, and a message is private in a way that a conversation across an open floor is not. This finding has been widely quoted and rather less widely acted upon, partly because the open plan solved a problem that was never about collaboration. It is considerably cheaper per employee. The more interesting response has come from firms that kept the open floor but added enough small enclosed rooms for anybody to take a conversation out of public hearing. Their conversation rates recovered. The lesson appears to be that people will talk in the open only when they have somewhere else to go.

questions.q: What was the open office promise?
options: Colleagues would talk more and ideas would travel
questions.note: "Remove the walls and colleagues will talk to one another."

questions.q: How was the promise tested?
options: Badges recorded who spoke to whom
questions.note: "Researchers fitted staff with badges that recorded who spoke to whom."

questions.q: What happened to face-to-face conversation?
options: It fell by about seventy per cent
questions.note: "Face-to-face conversation fell by roughly seventy per cent."

questions.q: Why did behavior change?
options: People became unwilling to be overheard
questions.note: "They had become less willing to be overheard."

questions.q: What worked for some firms?
questions.note: "Added enough small enclosed rooms... Their conversation rates recovered."

title: Müzelerin ödünç aldığı eserler
titleEn: The Exhibition That Traveled Too Far
text: A traveling exhibition looks generous. Objects that would otherwise be seen by the few thousand people who can reach one building are shown to hundreds of thousands across a continent. The cost of that generosity is rarely discussed outside the profession. Every journey exposes an object to changes in humidity and temperature, to vibration, and above all to handling, which is when almost all damage occurs. Conservators have a rule of thumb that the risk lies not in the flight but in the eleven separate occasions on which human hands lift the crate. Insurance covers the financial loss and can do nothing about the other kind. There is also a quieter effect. Objects that travel well are chosen repeatedly, so the same robust pieces tour while the fragile ones stay in storage, and the public's sense of what a collection contains is shaped by what survives a truck. Some museums have begun refusing loans for anything that has traveled twice in five years. The policy is unpopular with the institutions that want the object and, in the long run, is almost certainly correct.

questions.q: Where does most damage occur?
questions.note: "Above all to handling, which is when almost all damage occurs."

questions.q: What is the conservators' rule of thumb?
options: The risk is in the eleven liftings, not the flight
questions.note: "The risk lies not in the flight but in the eleven separate occasions."

questions.q: What is the quieter effect?
options: Robust pieces tour while fragile ones stay hidden
questions.note: "The same robust pieces tour while the fragile ones stay in storage."

questions.q: What have some museums begun doing?
options: Refusing loans for objects that traveled twice in five years
questions.note: "Refusing loans for anything that has traveled twice in five years."

questions.q: What is the writer's view of that policy?
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Kalabalıkla iş yapmak
titleEn: The Wisdom of the Crowd, and Its Limits
text: Ask a large group to estimate the weight of an ox and the average of their guesses will be close to the true figure, often closer than any expert. The experiment is famous and it is usually told as a story about the intelligence of crowds. It is really a story about independence. The average works because the individual errors point in different directions and cancel out, and that only happens when nobody hears anybody else's answer. Repeat the experiment while letting participants see the guesses already submitted and the accuracy collapses, because early answers pull later ones towards them and the errors stop being independent. This is not an obscure academic point. It describes what happens in a meeting where the most senior person speaks first, and it explains why written estimates collected before discussion routinely beat the number a group agrees on after an hour of debate. The practical instruction that follows is almost insultingly simple and almost never followed: ask everybody to write their answer down before anybody says anything out loud. The objection is always the same, that a meeting is for discussion and that writing things privately defeats the purpose. It does not. The written figures are the starting point rather than the conclusion, and the discussion that follows them is better informed precisely because it begins from a spread of genuinely separate opinions instead of a single number that everybody has already agreed to.

questions.q: Why does the average work?
questions.note: "The individual errors point in different directions and cancel out."

questions.q: What destroys the effect?
questions.note: "Letting participants see the guesses already submitted and the accuracy collapses."

questions.q: What does this explain about meetings?
options: Why the senior person speaking first is harmful
questions.note: "It describes what happens in a meeting where the most senior person speaks first."

questions.q: What beats a group's agreed number?
questions.note: "Written estimates collected before discussion routinely beat the number a group agrees on."

questions.q: What is the practical instruction?
options: Write answers down before anybody speaks
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Hastanede gece vardiyası
text: Hospital outcomes are measurably worse at night, and the reason is not that the staff on duty are less able. It is that almost every support around them thins out. Fewer senior doctors are on site, so a junior faces a decision alone that would be shared at noon. Test results take longer. The equipment is the same but the person who knows its particular failures has gone home. Add to this the biological cost of working against the body's own clock, which reduces accuracy in a way that no amount of professionalism prevents, and the gap becomes easy to explain and hard to close. The responses that work are unglamorous. A structured handover at every shift change, with a written form that cannot be skipped, is worth more than any appeal to vigilance. So is making it socially acceptable to telephone a senior at three in the morning, which sounds like a matter of policy and is really a matter of culture. Hospitals that have narrowed the night-time gap tend to describe the change in exactly those terms: not that they hired more people, but that nobody is now embarrassed to wake somebody up.

questions.q: Why are night outcomes worse?
options: The support around the staff thins out
questions.note: "Almost every support around them thins out."

questions.q: What does the body's clock do?
questions.note: "Reduces accuracy in a way that no amount of professionalism prevents."

questions.q: What is worth more than appeals to vigilance?
options: A structured handover that cannot be skipped
questions.note: "A structured handover at every shift change... is worth more than any appeal to vigilance."

questions.q: What does the writer call a matter of culture?
options: Being able to phone a senior at three
questions.note: "Sounds like a matter of policy and is really a matter of culture."

questions.q: How do successful hospitals describe the change?
options: Nobody is embarrassed to wake somebody up
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: İkinci el pazarının yükselişi
text: The market for used goods has grown faster than almost any part of retail, and the usual explanation is that buyers have become poorer or greener. Both are partly true and neither explains the shape of the growth. What changed was the removal of the two things that always made second-hand difficult: finding the item and trusting the seller. A search box solved the first. Ratings, photographs and a payment system that holds the money until the buyer confirms solved the second. Once those existed, the market grew into categories that nobody predicted, including furniture, which is expensive to move, and children's clothes, which are worn for weeks. There is an unresolved tension at the center of the business. Manufacturers benefit, because an item with a strong resale price is easier to sell new, and the buyer effectively borrows rather than buys. They also lose, because every used sale is a new one that did not happen. Most large firms have settled on a position that satisfies nobody: they run their own resale platforms, take a small fee, and quietly hope the whole thing stays small.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the usual explanations?
options: Partly true but they do not explain the shape
questions.note: "Both are partly true and neither explains the shape of the growth."

questions.q: What actually changed?
options: Finding items and trusting sellers became easy
questions.note: "The removal of the two things that always made second-hand difficult."

questions.q: What solved the trust problem?
questions.note: "Ratings, photographs and a payment system that holds the money."

questions.q: Why do manufacturers benefit?
options: A strong resale price helps sell new items
questions.note: "An item with a strong resale price is easier to sell new."

questions.q: What position have most large firms taken?
options: Run their own resale sites and hope it stays small
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Yapay ışığın bedeli
text: Cheap lighting was one of the clearest improvements of the last century, and like most clear improvements it was applied far past the point of usefulness. A street that is lit well enough to read a newspaper is lit considerably brighter than is needed to walk safely, and the extra brightness produces glare, which makes the dark places between lamps harder to see into rather than easier. The effect on wildlife is better documented than most people assume. Insects that navigate by the moon circle a lamp until they die, and the species that eat them follow the food and lose their own cycles. For human beings the measurable cost is to sleep, and it is caused less by the quantity of light than by its color: the blue-heavy light that is cheapest to produce is also the most effective at telling the body that the day has not ended. Several cities have quietly reduced their lighting at night and reported no rise in crime, which is the result nobody campaigns on because it is difficult to celebrate the absence of something. The cheapest improvement available is not to switch lights off but to point them down.

questions.q: What does extra brightness produce?
options: Glare that hides the dark places
questions.note: "The extra brightness produces glare."

questions.q: What happens to insects?
options: They circle a lamp until they die
questions.note: "Insects that navigate by the moon circle a lamp until they die."

questions.q: What causes the cost to human sleep?
questions.note: "Caused less by the quantity of light than by its color."

questions.q: What did several cities report?
options: No rise in crime after reducing lighting
questions.note: "Reported no rise in crime."

questions.q: What is the cheapest improvement?
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Ses kaydı ve hafıza
text: A growing number of people are recording conversations with elderly relatives, and the results are almost never what the recorder expected. The instinct is to ask about history: the war, the move, the hard years. Those answers tend to be the least useful, partly because they have been told so often that they have hardened into a fixed shape, and partly because the important detail has usually been polished away. The recordings that turn out to matter are the ones where nothing happens. A description of a kitchen. The names of four neighbors on a street that no longer exists. How much a bus cost and what the driver did when somebody could not pay. These are the things nobody thinks to preserve, because they seem too ordinary to lose, and they are exactly what disappears first. There is a practical difficulty. Most people begin recording after a diagnosis, which is the worst possible moment: the subject is tired, the family is frightened, and the recording carries a weight that makes ordinary talk impossible. The advice that archivists give is uncomfortable but consistent. Start ten years early, while it still feels unnecessary, and ask about a Tuesday rather than a decade.

questions.q: Why are the history answers least useful?
options: They have hardened into a fixed shape
questions.note: "They have been told so often that they have hardened into a fixed shape."

questions.q: Which recordings turn out to matter?
questions.note: "The recordings that turn out to matter are the ones where nothing happens."

questions.q: Why is the ordinary detail lost?
options: It seems too ordinary to lose
questions.note: "They seem too ordinary to lose, and they are exactly what disappears first."

questions.q: Why is starting after a diagnosis bad?
options: The recording carries a weight that stops ordinary talk
questions.note: "The recording carries a weight that makes ordinary talk impossible."

questions.q: What do archivists advise?
options: Start ten years early and ask about a Tuesday
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Turizmin iki yüzü
text: A coastal town of nine thousand people receives about four hundred thousand visitors a year, and the arithmetic of that produces effects that neither side of the argument describes accurately. The complaint that tourism destroys a place is too simple. Without the visitors the town would have the economy of the villages inland, which are emptying at a rate nobody defends. The claim that tourism saves a place is equally careless. The money arrives, but it arrives in a shape that the town cannot easily use: concentrated in fourteen weeks, spent mostly with firms registered elsewhere, and paid to staff who are themselves seasonal and leave in October. What the town is left with for the other thirty-eight weeks is a high street where two thirds of the units are shut and a housing market priced for people who are not there. The interventions that have worked in comparable places are unglamorous and local. A limit on how many properties in one street may be let to visitors. A requirement that a proportion of new building be sold only to residents. Neither policy attracts headlines, and both are considerably more effective than the debates that do.

questions.q: Why is the complaint too simple?
options: Without visitors the town would empty like the villages
questions.note: "Without the visitors the town would have the economy of the villages inland."

questions.q: What is wrong with the money that arrives?
options: It comes in a shape the town cannot use
There is too little of it
questions.note: "It arrives in a shape that the town cannot easily use."

questions.q: What is the town left with off-season?
options: Shut units and housing priced for absent people
questions.note: "Two thirds of the units are shut and a housing market priced for people who are not there."

questions.q: What kind of measures have worked?
questions.note: "The interventions that have worked... are unglamorous and local."

questions.q: What does the writer say about headlines?
options: The effective policies do not attract them
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Sınav kaygısı
text: Exam nerves are usually treated as a problem to be removed, and a great deal of advice is built on that assumption. The assumption is only half right. A moderate rise in heart rate before a test improves performance measurably; the body is preparing to concentrate, and students who report feeling nothing at all tend to do worse than those who report feeling slightly sick. What harms performance is not the sensation but the interpretation. A student who reads a fast heartbeat as evidence that they are about to fail enters a loop in which the fear produces the symptom and the symptom confirms the fear. Studies that simply tell students the physical meaning of what they are feeling, without any relaxation technique at all, produce a small but reliable improvement in results. This is a cheap intervention and it is rarely attempted, partly because it sounds too easy to be serious. It also has an obvious limit. Reframing works on ordinary nerves and does nothing for a student whose anxiety is severe enough to stop them entering the room, and treating those two situations as the same problem is the mistake that the confident advice usually makes.

questions.q: What does a moderate rise in heart rate do?
questions.note: "A moderate rise in heart rate before a test improves performance measurably."

questions.q: What actually harms performance?
questions.note: "What harms performance is not the sensation but the interpretation."

questions.q: What do the studies do?
options: Tell students the physical meaning of the feeling
questions.note: "Studies that simply tell students the physical meaning of what they are feeling."

questions.q: Why is the intervention rarely attempted?
options: It sounds too easy to be serious
questions.note: "Partly because it sounds too easy to be serious."

questions.q: What is the limit of the method?
options: It works only in one subject
It does nothing for severe anxiety
questions.note: "Reframing... does nothing for a student whose anxiety is severe."

title: Tamir hakkı
titleEn: The Right to Open the Case
text: For about two decades it became steadily harder to repair the things people own. Cases were glued rather than screwed, parts were paired to a single device by software, and repair manuals were treated as commercial secrets. The manufacturers' argument was safety, and it was not entirely dishonest: a badly repaired battery is genuinely dangerous. The argument was also extremely convenient, since the same policies produced a replacement cycle that no marketing department could have achieved on its own. The change now under way came from an unusual direction. Rather than banning the practices, several governments required firms to publish a repairability score on the packaging, in the same place as the energy rating. Scores are crude and can be gamed, and within two years the average score rose sharply, which suggests that the gaming was less effective than the embarrassment. The remaining obstacle is not law but skill. A generation has grown up without ever opening anything, and a repairable device is worth little to somebody who has never held a screwdriver. The countries making the most progress are the ones that funded repair workshops at the same time as the labels.

questions.q: What made repair harder?
options: Glued cases, paired parts and secret manuals
questions.note: "Cases were glued rather than screwed, parts were paired... manuals were treated as commercial secrets."

questions.q: What does the writer say about the safety argument?
options: Not entirely dishonest but very convenient
questions.note: "It was not entirely dishonest... The argument was also extremely convenient."

questions.q: What did several governments require?
options: A repairability score on the packaging
questions.note: "Required firms to publish a repairability score on the packaging."

questions.q: What does the rise in scores suggest?
questions.note: "The gaming was less effective than the embarrassment."

questions.q: What is the remaining obstacle?
questions.note: "The remaining obstacle is not law but skill."

title: Yeni bir şehirde arkadaşlık
text: People who move cities in their thirties are routinely surprised by how hard it is to make friends, having found it effortless at twenty. The explanation is not that adults are colder. Friendship reliably requires three conditions: repeated unplanned contact, a shared activity, and enough time in one another's company for the conversation to move past the subject that brought people together. School and university supply all three without anybody arranging anything. Adult life supplies the first only at work, where the relationship is complicated by the fact that both parties are being paid to be there and one of them may one day be reviewing the other. The practical conclusion is unromantic and it is the only one that reliably works. Friendship in adulthood has to be scheduled, which feels wrong to people who remember it happening by itself. The activity matters less than its regularity: a class that meets weekly for eight weeks will produce more genuine connection than eight separate interesting evenings with different people. Those who understand this tend to describe the first year in a new city as a project rather than a disappointment, and they are the ones who are still there in year three.

questions.q: What are the three conditions for friendship?
options: Unplanned contact, a shared activity, and time
questions.note: "Repeated unplanned contact, a shared activity, and enough time."

questions.q: Why is work an incomplete substitute?
options: Both are paid to be there and one may review the other
questions.note: "Both parties are being paid to be there and one of them may one day be reviewing the other."

questions.q: What is the practical conclusion?
options: Adult friendship has to be scheduled
questions.note: "Friendship in adulthood has to be scheduled."

questions.q: What matters more than the activity?
questions.note: "The activity matters less than its regularity."

questions.q: How do successful people describe the first year?
options: As a project rather than a disappointment
questions.note: Son cümle.
